title: SLO-driven configurations and cost sensitivity analysis
summary: Draft recommendations for selecting batching, caching and quantization settings keyed by customer SLO tiers and a cost-sensitivity matrix. Focused on pragmatic defaults, quick experiments, and guardrails for production rollouts.
body:
Purpose:
This doc is a lightweight, actionable draft that maps SLO tiers (latency and tail targets) to recommended inference configurations (batching, prefix/KV caching, quantization aggressiveness). It also includes a small cost-sensitivity matrix (text snapshot) and pragmatic experiment templates for the product/optimize and serving-runtime teams.

Context and constraints:
- Goal: reduce unit cost (per-request / per-token) while meeting p99/p95 latency SLOs and preserving output quality.
- Constraints: models vary (Llama2-like vs. transformer decoder variants), sequence length distributions differ per workload, and certain customers require private deployment (no shared cache).
- Risk profile: aggressive quantization and long-lived cache can cause quality regressions for some prompts. Recommend conservative canaries before rolling wide.

SLO-driven heuristic presets (quick defaults):
- Tier A: Tight SLO (p99 <= 200 ms, low p50 too)
  - Batch size target: 1 (no batching) or dynamic batching capped at 2 with immediate flush on interactive routes
  - Cache policy: KV/prefix caching disabled for latency-sensitive single-turn requests; ephemeral cache only for same-session short prefixes
  - Quantization: FP16 or fused 8-bit (dynamic) only; avoid 4-bit unless validated on eval set
  - Notes: prioritize single-request latency; scale horizontally (dedicated capacity) rather than batching.

- Tier B: Moderate SLO (p99 200-500 ms)
  - Batch size target: 2-4 (auto-batching with 20-50ms aggregation window)
  - Cache policy: short TTL prefix cache (30s-2min) for repeated prompts within a session; enable KV caching for multi-turn flows
  - Quantization: int8 dynamic for encoder/decoder parts where supported; test selective 4-bit for long-generation routes only
  - Notes: balance batching and cache to hit p99; prefer 2-4 batch for chat UIs.

- Tier C: Relaxed SLO / high throughput (p99 > 500 ms)
  - Batch size target: 8-16 (larger multi-request batches allowed)
  - Cache policy: aggressive prefix caching (TTL 5-15 min) and cross-request KV cache where privacy allows
  - Quantization: aggressive 4-bit / group-quantization and quantize attention kernels where supported
  - Notes: focus on throughput and cost; verify quality regressions on evaluation prompts.

Cost-sensitivity matrix (text snapshot) - baseline numbers are illustrative from internal experiments across two model families and a mixed query distribution. All costs are per 10k tokens equivalent served.

Columns: SLO_TIER | Batch | Cache_TTL | Quant_Mode | Est_cost_10k_base | Est_cost_10k_opt | Delta_pct | Expected_quality_impact
Tier A | 1 | 0s | FP16 | $28.40 | $26.90 | -5.3% | ~0%
Tier A | 1 | 0s | int8-dyn | $21.10 | $20.10 | -4.7% | small risk on rare prompts
Tier B | 4 | 60s | int8-dyn | $28.40 | $15.20 | -46.5% | low-moderate risk
Tier B | 4 | 60s | 4bit-hybrid | $28.40 | $11.30 | -60.2% | moderate risk, needs evals
Tier C | 12 | 600s | 4bit-aggr | $28.40 | $7.10 | -75.0% | noticeable quality delta on edge cases

Interpretation: batching and caching together yield the largest single wins for workloads with repeated prefixes or many short requests. Quantization compounds savings but increases quality risk non-linearly.

Experiment templates (quick A/B):
1) Tier B baseline vs auto-batching+30s cache
   - Metric: p99 latency, cost per 10k tokens, failure rate, model eval metric (BLEU/ROUGE/embedding-sim) on eval set
   - Duration: 48 hours or 100k requests
   - Stop condition: p99 regression > 10% or quality drift > 2% on eval set
2) 4-bit trial on long-generation subset
   - Target: routes with mean generation > 300 tokens
   - Rollout: canary 1% -> 5% -> 20% with automated rollback on quality regression

Guardrails and monitoring suggestions:
- Always pair quantization experiments with a small representative eval prompt set and embedding-similarity checks.
- Track unit cost delta broken down by token type (prompt vs generation) and by model variant.
- Add SLO-aware alerting: if cost drops but p99 increases beyond threshold, auto-enforce rollback.

Sample quick checklist before rollout:
- Run 1k eval prompts through quantized model; record per-prompt differences and percent of prompts with high delta (>0.2 in embedding sim)
- Smoke-test edge-case prompts (system messages, non-English, numeric-heavy)
- Validate fallback path: if KV cache lookup or quantized kernel fails, ensure automatic fallback to safe model variant

Notes on private deployments and tenant isolation:
- For private/VPC customers, caching strategies must be configurable per-tenant and default to conservative TTLs.
- Document any quantization-related export of runtime metrics that could leak information; keep telemetry minimal.

Estimated impact (conservative):
- For a chat workload with average request 80 tokens and 2-turn sessions, moving from Tier B baseline -> auto-batch(4)+30s cache+int8 yields ~40-55% cost reduction in production-like traffic.
- For high-throughput inference (Tier C) combining large batching + 4-bit quantization yields up to ~70% cost improvement but requires larger eval signal and careful rollout.

Open questions and uncertainties:
- How do we best quantify quality deltas across multilingual and code-generation prompts? Need expanded eval suites.
- Are there kernel-level latencies introduced by certain 4-bit paths that hurt tail latency more than batch-level averages suggest? Request infra team profiling.

References and quick links:
- Spreadsheet with raw experiment numbers: gsheet:cost-models-2025 (linked)
- Jira: OPT-789 (tracking rollout plan)
- Prior notes: confluence:optimize-guides
